source.title: The Surprising Effectiveness of Shared Memory in Looped Transformers
source.authors: Giovanni Monea; Keshav Ramji; Yousef El-Kurdi; Luis A. Lastras; Yoav Artzi; Nathan Godey; R. Astudillo

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether architectural choices change held-out language-model loss at matched parameter counts, but does not fit or evaluate scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper reports many parameter-count, recursion-count, architecture, and downstream-accuracy comparisons. Only its explicit matched-size architecture comparisons bearing on V4 are recorded here. It does not test power-law fits, extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation, or downstream predictability.
record.test_reason: The DEEPSTD baseline is a deeper, narrower, approximately parameter-matched standard Transformer at 2, 3, 5 and 9 times the depth. It is trained on the same data and tokens as STD, so it bears on V4 (shape at fixed parameters). The looped-model comparisons the reader recorded do not test V4: looping adds about 4–5x compute per token, and memory sharing is a cache and attention-pattern change, not a shape change.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that trained memory sharing in looped Transformers cuts context memory and also improves perplexity and accuracy over matched looped baselines. The hybrid H-LPT beats a same-size STD with 76–79% less context memory. Gains are attributed to role specialisation of recursions and a gradient highway to the first recursion.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares looped, shared-memory, hybrid, and standard architectures; it does not fit scaling laws or reproduce the original scaling-law methods.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported loss comparisons vary with architecture, model size, and recursion count. The paper also reports effects of training objective, prediction-window size, and normalization, but does not test their effects on fitted scaling laws.

fits_no_version.finding: At matched parameters, looped models with extra recursions (extra compute per token) lower perplexity by up to 1.92 vs STD. Memory sharing lowers perplexity by 0.38–1.09 vs LT at matched compute.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: At fixed parameter count, adding compute per token through weight-shared recursion lowers language-model loss, and cache-sharing design changes how much.

record.problems: The main comparison uses one run per configuration; additional seeds and statistical tests are reported for S-size models. The architecture comparisons do not constitute a controlled broad sweep of depth and width.
record.rows_left_out: Individual Table 1 values for model, size, and recursion combinations are not transcribed; the explicit aggregate comparisons in Sections 5 and Table 1 are retained for V4.

untested.parts: Width-only, head-count and FFN-ratio variation. Shapes shallower or wider than STD. Exact parameter matching: DEEPSTD is only approximately matched and its dimensions are not given.

missing.what: DEEPSTD (deeper, narrower, parameter-matched standard Transformer) vs STD validation perplexity at R=2,3,5,9 depth multiples for S, M and L
missing.locator: Table 1 STD rows (R>1 = DEEPSTD); Table 7; Table 3 (S seeds: 17.03/17.27/17.64 vs 16.84)

record.verdict_notes: Loss percentages for DEEPSTD are my calculation from reported perplexities (loss = ln ppl); the authors do not frame DEEPSTD as a shape test. DEEPSTD has one run per size except S, where four seeds confirm the gap (Table 3). Training runs 2–7x past Chinchilla token budgets, with untuned nanoGPT optimizer settings for all models. The deeper models may be disadvantaged by untuned hyperparameters. The reader's 'challenges' label on V4 should be dropped.

versions.untested_parts: Power-law loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute; several orders of magnitude; bottleneck conditions.
Fitting laws on smaller runs and predicting much larger runs.
Finding loss-minimising parameter/token allocations at fixed compute and their trends with compute.
A broad controlled sweep of depth, width, and other architecture details; the reported comparisons are specific looped, hybrid, and standard architectures.
Other modalities and training regimes, including repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer.
Predicting downstream performance from scale or pretraining loss; downstream scores are reported but not analyzed as a predictive scaling relationship.
Dependence of scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocation on fitting choices, and bending of scaling curves.

rows.subject: LPT
rows.operation_detail: Compared five-recursion LPT with same-size standard Transformer

conditions.value: 20B for S and M; 50B for L

rows.uncertainty: not stated for this aggregate comparison
rows.locator: Section 5, More Quality from the Same Parameters; Table 1
rows.note: Aggregate range reported by the paper across sizes; demonstrates a larger-than-slight loss difference for the tested architecture comparison.
rows.check: LPT with five recursions uses 4.3–4.8x STD's FLOPs. Matched parameters but unmatched compute is not a shape comparison, so the perplexity gain does not bear on V4. Fed into a wrong 'challenges' label.

rows.subject: H-LPT
rows.operation_detail: Compared five-recursion hybrid H-LPT with same-size standard Transformer

conditions.value: 20B for S and M; 50B for L

rows.uncertainty: not stated for this aggregate comparison
rows.locator: Section 5, More Quality from the Same Parameters; Table 1
rows.note: Aggregate range reported by the paper across sizes; demonstrates a larger-than-slight loss difference for the tested architecture comparison.
rows.check: H-LPT with five recursions uses about 3.75x STD's FLOPs and is a hybrid with linear attention. The gain reflects extra compute and a different attention type, not depth or width at fixed compute.

rows.subject: LPT
rows.operation_detail: Compared LPT with matched-size, matched-recursion LT

conditions.value: 20B for S and M; 50B for L

rows.uncertainty: not stated for this aggregate comparison
rows.locator: Section 5, Memory Sharing Improves Quality; Table 1
rows.note: Aggregate range across matched sizes and recursion counts; the comparison changes the looped architecture by adding trained memory sharing.
rows.check: LPT vs LT changes cache sharing inside a looped model, not shape. The LT baseline is also unstable under Ouro's normalization (Appendix C), so the gap is not a test of whether architecture details matter slightly.

relationships.condition: DEEPSTD at 2–5x STD depth (narrower, about parameter-matched), S/M/L, 20B/50B tokens
relationships.reason: Text-based, no row: Table 1 STD R>1 perplexities rise only 0.24–0.92 over STD (S 16.83→17.07–17.69; L 11.35→11.62–12.27). That is about 2–3% in loss (ln ppl).
relationships.display_finding: Perplexity rose from 16.83 to 17.07–17.69 for small models and from 11.35 to 11.62–12.27 for large models, corresponding to about 2–3% higher loss.

relationships.condition: DEEPSTD at 9x depth, M and L sizes
relationships.reason: Text-based, no row: Table 7 gives M 13.79→15.60 and L 11.35→12.66. That is about 4.5–4.7% higher loss, and the gap grows steadily with depth.
relationships.display_finding: Perplexity increased from 13.79 to 15.60 for medium models and from 11.35 to 12.66 for large models, corresponding to about 4.5–4.7% higher loss.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Reported matched-size architecture comparisons, including five-recursion LPT and H-LPT versus STD
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports validation-perplexity reductions of 1.03–1.92 for LPT and 1.12–1.82 for H-LPT relative to same-size STD, rather than only slight architecture-related changes (r1, r2). The matched-depth LPT–LT comparison also reports reductions of 0.38–1.09 (r3).
